title: warmup-robustness-matrix-and-anchor-scenarios
summary: Working notes and actionable checklist for constructing a warmup-robustness matrix: a small suite of anchor scenarios + repeatability hygiene to validate throughput numbers across kernels, sequence lengths, and cache states.
content:
Purpose:
This document is a working checklist and experiment matrix for validating that our throughput harness produces stable, repeatable throughput numbers across a variety of warmup and priming strategies. Goal is to reduce flakiness in benchmark results and surface sensitivity to: RNG/entropy, KV cache state, batch packing, and background noise (OS/GPU throttling).

High-level approach (short):
- Define a compact set of anchor scenarios that exercise distinct runtime paths (short vs long seq, batched vs single-stream, KV-heavy vs KV-light).
- For each anchor, apply a set of warmup recipes (cold, staircase-priming, randomized jitter priming, full-cache prefill).
- Run N independent repeats with controlled seeds and capture full trace + system telemetry.
- Post-process to extract steady-state windows, compute CI on throughput, and flag runs with >3% within-scenario variance.

Anchor scenario matrix (recommended minimal set):
1) anchor-text-short-unbatched:
   - seq_len_target: 48 tokens
   - batch_size: 1
   - concurrency: 4 streams
   - kv_cache: empty on start

2) anchor-text-short-batched:
   - seq_len_target: 48 tokens
   - batch_size: 8
   - concurrency: 8 total inflight (CBR-style)
   - kv_cache: empty on start

3) anchor-long-context-batched:
   - seq_len_target: 2048 tokens (or model max if lower)
   - batch_size: 4
   - concurrency: 2
   - kv_cache: progressive growth — requests contain repeated prefixes to populate KV

4) anchor-kv-heavy-mixed:
   - mixed sequence lengths: 64/512/1024 with probability 0.6/0.3/0.1
   - batch_size: 4
   - concurrency: chosen to target ~75% GPU occupancy in steady-state
   - kv_cache: warm (pre-populated from replay corpus)

Warmup recipes (executable patterns):
- cold-no-priming: start harness against freshly restarted infer-server, do not send warmup requests. Capture cold-start behavior.
- staircase-priming (recommended baseline): ramp qps in geometric steps (e.g., 10%, 25%, 50%, 75%, target) holding 30–90s per step then hold target for 5m. Purpose: let allocators and kernels stabilize.
- randomized-jitter-priming: send mix of short and long requests with random inter-arrival jitter (0–100ms) for 5–10 minutes. Catch pathological scheduling interactions.
- full-cache-prefill: replay N representative requests to populate KV cache before measurement window. Useful for KV-sensitive models.

Repeatability hygiene (must-haves for each experiment):
- RNG seeds: record and (where possible) fix client-side RNG for input sampling and loadgen. Include run_id seed in metadata.
- Host env snapshot: capture kernel version, nvidia-smi output, GPU clocks, CPU governor, watched processes.
- Deterministic artifacts: use pinned model binary + kernel set. Record commit hash for serving-runtime and model artifact version.
- Warmup log: store warmup timeline and any step transitions.
- Minimum repeats: 10 independent repeats for short anchors, 5 for long-run anchors (practical). Repeats must be run at different wall-clock times to catch diurnal noise.

Measurement windows and steady-state selection:
- Capture full time-series at 1s granularity for throughput and latency metrics.
- Discard a safety headroom interval (first 60–180s) depending on warmup recipe.
- Identify steady-state by checking throughput slope: require |d(throughput)/dt| < 0.2%/s over a 60s window. If not found, mark run as unstable.
- Use 95% confidence intervals across repeats (bootstrap recommended) and report median + CI.

Loadgen config snippets (examples to copy):
- client flags: --run-id=<id> --seed=<seed> --target-qps=<qps> --arrival-distribution=poisson --jitter-ms=10 --payload-profile=anchor-short
- payload profiles: stored in /bench/payloads/*, name matches anchor id. Keep payloads small (sampled real prefixes).

Observability and instrumentation (what to collect):
- server: per-request latency histogram (buckets up to model max), token throughput, batch size distribution, kernel selection log (if available), memory allocator stats, KV cache hit ratio.
- infra: gpu_util, gpu_power_watts, gpu_mem_used, cpu_load, interrupted context switches, page faults.
- network: p50/p95 request path RTTs between loadgen and server; ensure not network-bound.
- tracing: link request ids across loadgen -> gateway -> runtime to stitch per-request timelines.

Post-run analyses (recommended):
- throughput time-series plot with annotated warmup steps.
- occupancy vs throughput heatmap: x=effective sequence length occupancy, y=batch size, color=throughput. Helps identify packing cliffs.
- latency tail regression: compare p95/p99 across repeats and anchor variants; correlate with batch size distribution and kernel changes.
- CI table: median throughput + 95% CI + CV for each anchor/warmup combination. Flag CV > 3% for investigation.

Failure modes and quick triage (checklist):
- if throughput sudden drop during run:
  - confirm no node autoscaling event or tenant eviction
  - check GPU thermal throttle (nvidia-smi dmon, driver logs)
  - inspect batch size distribution: observed spike in tiny batches -> upstream client pacing issue
- if steady-state not reached:
  - lengthen staircase steps or add extra ramp stages
  - try full-cache-prefill to remove cold-KV noise
- high variance across repeats:
  - check for non-deterministic kernel selector (record selection coupling to input shapes)
  - investigate system-level noise (others processes, cron jobs)

Artifacts naming and storage policy:
- run_id template: <date>-<anchor>-<warmup>-<seed>-<iter> (e.g., 2025-02-03-anchor-long-context-batched-s123-03)
- store raw traces in s3://redwood-bench/throughput-raw/<run_id>.tar.gz
- store derived artifacts (plots, CSV summaries) in s3://redwood-bench/throughput-processed/<run_id>/

Practical notes and heuristics learned (tribal knowledge):
- small differences in GPU clocking policies between nodes can produce 1–3% throughput shifts; include a node-compatibility check in smoke runs.
- KV-heavy workloads are very sensitive to input alignment: two logically similar inputs can produce different kernel paths; watch for subtle distribution drift.
- Stochastic priming (randomized-jitter) often uncovers scheduling regressions that staircase misses. Run both.

Next actions / TODOs:

- (Evan) add automatic steady-state detector to bench postproc and fail runs that don’t reach steady-state.
- (Priya) curate 20 representative payloads for full-cache-prefill for kv-heavy models.
- schedule 2-week run sweep across the anchor matrix and collect baseline for Q1 release notes.

- Confluence: Warmup patterns playbook (internal)

Notes to self / experiment log (scratch):

- 2025-01-27: randomized-jitter found a case where batcher produced 3x tiny batches for a 1s interval. Root cause: upstream pacing jitter and packer timeout interaction.

End.
